label: thm:Db
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:Db}
For $j\in\mathbb N_0$,
$$ b_j = (|\mu| - e)^{*j}. $$
The corresponding Dirichlet series has the form
\[
\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{b_j}{n^s}=\left ( \frac{\zeta(s)}{\zeta(2s)}-1\right)^j
\qquad (\mathop{\rm Re} s > 1).
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
From equation (\ref{lembj})
\begin{align*}
 b_j(n) &= \lambda(n) \sum_{n_1 n_2 \cdots n_j = n} \prod_{k=1}^j (\mu(n_k) - e(n_k))
 = \sum_{n_1 n_2 \cdots n_j = n} \prod_{k=1}^j \lambda(n_k) (\mu(n_k) - e(n_k))
 & \\
 &= \sum_{n_1 n_2 \cdots n_j = n} \prod_{k=1}^j (|\mu(n_k)| - e(n_k))
 = (|\mu| - e)^{*j}(n)
\qquad (n\in\mathbb N),
 \end{align*}
where we used the complete multiplicativity of
$\lambda$
and the facts that
$\lambda \mu = |\mu|$
and
$\lambda e = e.$

For the Dirichlet series, we first note that for a general arithmetic function $f(n)$ with Dirichlet series $F(s)$, the arithmetic function $f(n)-e(n)$ has Dirichlet series
\[
\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{f(n)-e(n)}{n^s}=\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{f(n)}{n^s}-1=F(s)-1.
\]
Also, the Dirichlet series of a convolution of arithmetic functions is equal
to the product of their individual Dirichlet series.
Hence the $j$-th convolution power $(f(n)-e(n))^{*j}$ has Dirichlet series $(F(s)-1)^j$.

The Dirichlet series for Liouville's function $\lambda$ is given by $\zeta(2s)/\zeta(s)$ \cite{Lehman}.
Moreover, the Dirichlet convolution inverse of $\lambda$ is
the absolute value of the Möbius function \cite[Ex.\ I.8.(8)]{rSchSp},
$\lambda^{-*}(n) = \mu(n)\,\lambda(n) = |\mu(n)| = \mu^2(n)$, which is the characteristic function of the squarefree integers.

It follows that the function $(|\mu| - e)$ has the Dirichlet series $\zeta(s)/\zeta(2s)-1$ (see also \cite[Corollary 8.20]{NZM}), and consequently
\[
\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{b_j(n)}{n^s}=\left ( \frac{\zeta(s)}{\zeta(2s)}-1\right)^j.
\qedhere
\]
head: environment

label: eq:Dbal
title: Remark
body_md:
In view of equation (\ref{eq:bdef}),                                                  
it is of interest to compare this with the
Dirichlet series for $c_j^{(-j)}$
(see \cite{mcl4}),
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Dbal}
\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{c_j^{(-j)}(n)}{n^s} = \left (1-\frac{1}{\zeta(s)}\right )^j.
\end{equation}

label: defn:1
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{defn:1}
The {\it non-trivial and balanced divisor function polynomials\/} are defined for $n\in\mathbb N$ and $x\in\mathbb C$ as
\[
P(n,x)=\sum_{j=1}^\infty x^{j-1}c_j(n),\qquad Q(n,x)=\sum_{j=1}^\infty x^{j-1}c_j^{(-j)}(n),
\]
respectively.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
As an immediate consequence, the non-trivial and balanced divisor function polynomials are the generating functions for the respective divisor functions, satisfying
\[
\frac{1}{(k-1)!}\,\frac{\partial^{k-1}}{\partial x^{k-1}}P(n,0) =c_k(n),\quad
\frac{1}{(k-1)!}\,\frac{\partial^{k-1}}{\partial x^{k-1}}Q(n,0) =c_k^{(-k)}(n).
\]

label: thm112
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By the definition of Dirichlet convolution, we see that for every arithmetic
function $f$,
\begin{equation*}
\sum_{d | n,\ d < n} f(d) = (f * (1 - e))(n) \qquad (n\in\mathbb N).
\end{equation*}
Hence the right-hand side of equation (\ref{115}), abstracting from the variable
$n$, is equal to
\begin{align*}
 (x\, P(\cdot, x) + e) * (1 - e) &= x\,P(\cdot, x) * (1 - e) + e * (1 - e)
\\
 &= x \sum_{j=1}^\infty x^{j-1}\,c_j * (1 - e) + 1 - e
\\
 &= \sum_{j=1}^\infty x^j\,(1 - e)^{*(j+1)} + 1 - e
 = \sum_{k=2}^\infty x^{k-1}\,(1 - e)^{*k} + 1 - e
\\
 &= \sum_{k=1}^\infty x^{k-1}\,(1 - e)^{*k}
 = P(\cdot, x).
\end{align*}
Equation (\ref{116}) now follows by Theorem \ref{thm11} as
\begin{align*}
 Q(\cdot, x) &= P(\cdot, x - 1)
 = ((x - 1) P(\cdot, x - 1) + e) * (1 - e)
\\
 &= ((x - 1) Q(\cdot, x) + e) * (1 - e).
\end{align*}
Finally, as the Dirichlet series of a convolution of arithmetic functions
is the product of their separate Dirichlet series, we
deduce from equation (\ref{eq:DPQ}) that
\begin{align*}
P(n, x) &= \left((P(\cdot, x) + e) * Q(\cdot, x)\right)(n)
= \sum_{d | n} (P(d, x) + e(d))\,Q\left(\frac n d, x\right)
\end{align*}
for all $n\in\mathbb N$, giving equation (\ref{117}) since
$Q(1, x) = 0$.
head: environment

label: corcom
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{corcom}
The polynomial sequence $(|P(n,-2)|)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ gives the number of all ordered factorisations of $n$ into squarefree numbers greater than 1 (cf.\ OEIS A050328);
more precisely, for $n\in\mathbb N$,
\begin{align*}
 P(n, -2) &= Q(n, -1)
 = \sum_{j=1}^\infty (-1)^{j-1} c_j^{(-j)}(n)
 = \sum_{j=1}^\infty (-1)^{j-1} (-1)^j \lambda(n)\,b_j(n)
\\
 &= (-1)^{\Omega(n)+1} \sum_{j=1}^\infty b_j(n).
\end{align*}
Taking $x = -1$, we find
\begin{equation*}
P(n, -1) = Q(n, 0) = c_1^{(-1)}(n) = (e - \mu)(n),
\end{equation*}
so, except at $n = 1$, its values are the negative of the M\"obius function
(cf.\ the sequence OEIS A008683).
The sequence $(P(n,0))_{n\in\mathbb N}$ is the sequence with every term (except for the leading 0) equal to 1 (cf.\ OEIS A000012),
since $P(n, 0) = c_1(n) = (1 - e)(n)$. Interestingly, by Theorem \ref{thm11}
this implies that
\begin{equation*}
 Q(n, 1) = \sum_{j=1}^\infty c_j^{(-j)}(n) = 1 \qquad (n \in \mathbb N, n \ge 2)
\end{equation*}
(cf.\ \cite[Eq. (7) with $r = 1$]{mcl4}).
Similarly, the sequence $(P(n,1))_{n \in\mathbb N}$ corresponds to the number of ordered factorisations of $n$ into integers greater than 1 (cf.\ OEIS A074206), which accords with the total number of perfect partitions of $n$ (see OEIS A002033).

Regarding $P(n, r)$ with $r \ge 2$, we note that its Dirichlet series (\ref{eq:DP}) coincides with that given in the Online Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences for the counts of ``ordered factorisations with increasing levels of parenthesis''
(e.g. see for parenthesis levels $1,2$ and $3$ respectively, the OEIS A050354, A050356 and A050358).
It is also remarked there that
the parenthesis level $r$ sequence $(a(n))_{n\in\mathbb N}$ satisfies the
recurrence relation
\[
a(n)=r\sum_{d\mid n,\ d<n}a(d)\quad (n\geq 2), \qquad a(1)=\frac{1}{r},
\]
which is consistent with Equation (\ref{115}) setting
$a(n) = P(n, r) + e(n)/r$,
and further that the partial sums of terms has asymptotic
\[
\sum_{n=1}^m \left (P(n,r)+e(n)\right )\asymp \frac{m^k}{r^2\, k\,\zeta^\prime(k)},
\]
where $k$ is such that $\zeta(k)=1+\frac{1}{k}$
(cf.\ the definition of $r_m$ in Theorem \ref{thm:DN} below).

title: Definition
body_md:
The {\it Bernoulli numbers\/} $B_n$ form a special sequence of rational numbers which are related to the Riemann zeta function at even integer arguments. The sequence begins $(B_0, B_1, B_2, B_3, B_4, B_5, B_6, \dots) = (1,-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{6},0,-\frac{1}{30},0,\frac{1}{42},\dots)$, defined by the generating function \cite[p.\ 48]{comtet}
\[
\frac{t}{e^t-1}=\sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{t^n B_n}{n!};
\]
there is also the historic variant \cite[p.\ 107]{conway}
\[
\frac{t e^t}{e^t-1}=\sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{t^n B_n^+}{n!},
\]
where $B_n^+=B_n$ for $n\neq 1$, $B_1^+=\frac{1}{2}$.

The {\it ordered Bell numbers\/} (or {\it Fubini numbers\/}) $F_n$,  and {\it ordered Bell polynomials\/} $F_n(x)$ are defined by
\[
F_n=\sum_{k=1}^nk!S(nk),\quad \text{and}\quad F_n(x)=\sum_{k=1}^nk!S(n,k)x^k,
\]
respectively,
where $S(n,k)$ are the Stirling numbers of the second kind. The ordered Bell numbers count the number of weak orderings or equivalently the number of distinct \emph{ordered} partitions of a set of $n$ elements \cite{tanny}.

Lastly, we define the {\it signed ordered Bell numbers\/} $F_n^-$ and {\it signed ordered Bell polynomials\/} $F_n^-(x)$ as
\[
F_n^-=\sum_{k=1}^n(-1)^{n-k}k!S(n,k)\quad \text{and}\quad F_n^-(x)=\sum_{k=1}^n(-1)^{n-k}k!S(n,k)x^k.
\]

label: thm115
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm115}
Let $n$ be a squarefree number with $\omega(n)=\Omega(n)$ distinct prime factors. Then
\[
x\,P(n,x)=F_{\omega(n)}(x),\qquad x\,Q(n,x)=F^-_{\omega(n)}(x).
\]
head: environment

label: eq:sff
title: Proof
body_md:
Every non-trivial divisor of the squarefree number $n$ is also squarefree, so the
number of non-trivial factorisations of $n$ is equal to the number of
non-trivial squarefree factorisations, i.e.\ $b_j(n) = c_j(n)$.
Moreover, factorising $n$ into $j$ non-trivial factors is equivalent to
assigning its $\Omega(n) = \omega(n)$ prime factors to $j$ non-empty sets,
with each non-trivial factor being the (commutative) product of the primes in
one of the sets. Hence
\begin{equation}\label{eq:sff}
c_j(n) = |c_j^{(-j)}(n)| = b_j(n) = S(\omega(n), j)\,j!.
\end{equation}
It follows that
\begin{equation*}
x\,P(n, x) = \sum_{j=1}^{\omega(n)} x^j\,c_j(n)
 = \sum_{j=1}^{\omega(n)} x^j\,j!\,S(\omega(n), j)
 = F_{\omega(n)}(x).
\end{equation*}
Similarly,
\begin{align*}
x\,Q(n, x) &= \sum_{j=1}^{\omega(n)} x^j\,c_j^{(-j)}(n)
 = \sum_{j=1}^{\omega(n)} x^j\,(-1)^{j+\omega(n)}\,b_j(n)
\\
 &= \sum_{j=1}^{\omega(n)} x^j\,(-1)^{j+\omega(n)}\,S(\omega(n), j)\,j!
 = F_{\omega(n)}^-(x).
\qedhere
\end{align*}
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
We note that, by equations (\ref{enum22}) and (\ref{eq:sff}), the number of $m$-part sum systems when $n$ is squarefree is given by
\[
 {\mathcal N}_m(n) =
m!\sum_{L=0}^{\omega{(n)}}(-1)^{\omega(n)+L} \,L!\, S(L,m)\, S(\omega(n),L).
\]
head: environment

title: Corollary
body_md:
Let $n$ be a squarefree natural number. Then
\begin{align*}
P\left(n,x-\frac{1}{2}\right)&=(-1)^{\omega(n)-1}P\left(n,-x-\frac{1}{2}\right),
\\
 Q\left(n,x+\frac{1}{2}\right)&=(-1)^{\omega(n)-1}Q\left(n,-x+\frac{1}{2}\right) \qquad (x \in \mathbb C).
\end{align*}
In particular, the zeros of $P(n, \cdot)$ and the zeros of $Q(n, \cdot)$ are
point symmetric around $\frac 12$ and $-\frac 12$, respectively.

title: Remark
body_md:
At a casual glance, the first term in the formula
\cite[equation (1.7)]{ivic}
\[
\zeta(s)=\frac{s}{s-1}+s\int_1^\infty([t]-t)t^{-s-1}\, d t \qquad (s > 1)
\]
would suggest that $r_m \approx m$; however, the inequality in Theorem \ref{thm:DN} shows that the integral term causes a considerable adjustment.
A good estimate of the integral could lead to a better bound for $r_m$.
